stories.headline: NASDAQ 100 SLIDES INTO CORRECTION AS CHIP AND MEMORY STOCKS TUMBLE ON AI CAPEX DOUBTS
stories.body: The NDX fell roughly 1% Tuesday to about 27,760, pushing the index more than 10% below its recent record and into correction territory; Dell Technologies dropped 8% and Intel fell 6% as the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index posted its fourth straight losing session, with investors increasingly skeptical that AI infrastructure spending will generate returns to match the buildout.
stories.explain: A 'correction' is simply a 10%-plus drawdown from a recent peak - a line traders watch closely because it often triggers systematic selling from funds with drawdown limits, turning a sentiment shift into forced flows. The proximate trigger is capital efficiency doubt: chipmakers and hyperscalers have been capitalizing enormous GPU spending as long-lived assets, and any sign that AI workloads generate less revenue per dollar of capex than assumed forces the market to reprice depreciation-heavy earnings streams lower. That question gets tested directly this week - Microsoft and Meta report Wednesday, Apple and Amazon Thursday - and their capex guidance will do more to resolve or worsen this selloff than anything said at Wednesday's Fed decision.

stories.headline: FOMC OPENS TWO-DAY MEETING UNDER CHAIR KEVIN WARSH AS DOLLAR HOLDS AT A ONE-MONTH HIGH
stories.body: The Federal Reserve began its July 28-29 meeting - Warsh's second as chair since replacing Jerome Powell in May - with the fed funds rate expected to hold at 3.50%-3.75% Wednesday at 2 p.m. ET, even as futures still price roughly a one-third chance of a surprise hike; the dollar index held near 101.55, its highest level in a month, on the lingering hawkish risk.
stories.explain: Futures-implied hike odds this elevated for a meeting widely expected to end in a hold reflect genuine uncertainty about how Warsh's reaction function differs from Powell's - markets are still calibrating how much weight a new chair puts on the oil-driven CPI prints from earlier this year against the growth risk a hike would add. A firmer dollar heading into a Fed decision typically signals the market pricing hawkish scenarios more heavily than dovish ones, since a hike (or a hold paired with hawkish language) draws in yield-seeking capital. Wednesday's post-meeting statement language, more than the vote itself, will move cross-asset pricing given how close the tail-risk odds are running into decision day.

stories.headline: WTI CRUDE SINKS TOWARD $79, 10-YEAR YIELD FALLS TO A ONE-WEEK LOW AS IRAN TALKS PROGRESS
stories.body: WTI crude fell about 4% to roughly $79 a barrel and Brent slid toward $87 as U.S. and Iranian officials resumed high-level talks, unwinding more of the war-risk premium built up earlier this month; the 10-year Treasury yield fell for a third straight session to 4.62%, its lowest level in about a week, as easing energy prices reinforced the case for a Fed hold.
stories.explain: Oil's fast pass-through to headline inflation is the direct link between a single day's crude move and Treasury pricing: falling energy costs lower near-term CPI expectations, which increases demand for duration and pulls yields down even before any Fed action. Three consecutive sessions of yield declines heading into a Fed decision is a meaningful signal - it shows bond markets pricing rising confidence in a hold, not just noise around one data point. The risk to this trade is a partial reversal if Wednesday's statement reads more hawkish than the one-third hike odds currently priced, since a chunk of today's yield move was about softer oil as much as a softer Fed.

stories.headline: BIG TECH'S CAPEX-HEAVY EARNINGS WEEK ARRIVES WITH MICROSOFT AND META REPORTING WEDNESDAY
stories.body: Microsoft and Meta report Wednesday, followed by Apple and Amazon Thursday, with investors focused less on headline beats and more on capital-expenditure guidance after Alphabet's capex disclosures last week rattled the market and helped trigger this week's chip-stock selloff; Meta separately announced a $14 billion deal with BlackRock to help fund a 1-gigawatt Texas data center.
stories.explain: Wall Street cares more about capex guidance than trailing revenue right now because heavy AI infrastructure spending shows up first as depreciation and lower free cash flow, and only later - if ever - as matching revenue, so guidance is the market's best forward read on whether that gap is closing or widening. Alphabet's disclosure moved markets last week precisely because it revised the multi-year spending trajectory upward without a commensurate revenue revision, the exact pattern investors are now bracing for from Microsoft and Meta. A structure like Meta's BlackRock joint venture - keeping a data center off Meta's own balance sheet - is itself a tell that hyperscalers are trying to keep gross capex from fully hitting their own reported free cash flow.

stories.headline: GOLD RETREATS TOWARD $4,046 AS A FIRMER DOLLAR PRESSURES THE METAL AHEAD OF THE FED
stories.body: Gold fell about 1.1% to roughly $4,046 an ounce as the dollar held near a one-month high, raising the metal's cost for overseas buyers just as investors position for Wednesday's FOMC decision.
stories.explain: Gold and the dollar share an inverse mechanical relationship because gold is priced in dollars: a firmer greenback makes bullion costlier in other currencies, curbing foreign buying and pushing the dollar price down independent of any change in underlying demand for gold as a safe-haven or inflation hedge. That the metal is falling into a Fed meeting where markets still assign real odds to a hike shows real, not just nominal, yield expectations are working against gold, since bullion carries no yield of its own and looks less attractive whenever real rates are expected to rise. A sustained break below $4,000 would signal the market treating a hold as fully priced rather than merely likely.

stories.headline: COLLEGE BASKETBALL'S ELIGIBILITY FIGHT NOW SPANS THREE STATES AS TRANSFER CHAOS CONTINUES
stories.body: A sprawling eligibility dispute is being litigated in three states on behalf of more than 80 combined plaintiffs, with resolution expected before the season opens, likely in August; the fight follows a record transfer-portal window that sent more than 2,700 players searching for new teams after the 2025-26 season, while Illinois signed a five-year, $30 million jersey patch deal with Busey Bank.

stories.headline: NUGGETS OFFER RESTRICTED FREE AGENT PEYTON WATSON $70 MILLION AS BUCKS WEIGH A MATCH
stories.body: Denver extended forward Peyton Watson a five-year, $70 million offer sheet, with Milwaukee viewed as the favorite to retain him using a $25.5 million trade exception if the Nuggets' offer is matched or worked around; elsewhere, Cleveland and James Harden are negotiating a new deal expected to run no more than two years.

stories.headline: EAGLES MAKE JALEN CARTER THE NFL'S HIGHEST-PAID DEFENSIVE TACKLE WITH A $152 MILLION EXTENSION
stories.body: Philadelphia locked up Pro Bowl defensive tackle Jalen Carter through 2031 on a four-year, $152 million extension worth up to $160 million with incentives, including $106 million guaranteed, surpassing Jeffery Simmons as the NFL's highest-paid interior defender, as all 32 teams opened training camp this week.

stories.headline: COURT INJUNCTION RESTORES NORTHWESTERN CENTER JACKSON CARSELLO'S ELIGIBILITY FOR 2026
stories.body: A court injunction restored Northwestern center Jackson Carsello's eligibility for the 2026 season after the NCAA denied his waiver request this spring, the latest eligibility case to land in the courts as fall camps open nationally; Big Ten Media Days run Tuesday-Thursday this week in Chicago.

sports.detail: Recruiting is the headline again this week as in-state prospect Censere Gaylord committed alongside 4-star cornerback and 4-star safety pledges; Jedd Fisch continues calling plays himself after February's coordinator departure. The Huskies open the season Sunday, Sept. 6, at home against Washington State.

Danny Sprinkle is rebuilding after a 16-17 season (7-13 Big Ten) and the June departure of leading scorer Hannes Steinbach, taken 14th overall by the Charlotte Hornets in the NBA Draft; the Huskies are still chasing their first NCAA tournament bid since 2019.

The defending Super Bowl champions opened camp with a public practice Tuesday and no new injury news; the team is reportedly parting ways with RB Kenny McIntosh as the backfield is reshaped, with Tennessee's Tony Pollard floated as a trade target. Seattle opens the season Sept. 9 at home against New England in a Super Bowl LX rematch, with the champions' banner raised beforehand.

Detroit's Summer League run is wrapping up in Las Vegas as the front office remains at a stalemate with restricted free agent Jalen Duren over a new contract; the offseason picture around the East got louder this week with LeBron James signing with Philadelphia.

Seattle dropped the finale in Arlington as Joc Pederson homered twice and drove in four runs for Texas, with Ezequiel Duran and Jake Burger also going deep; the Mariners head to Los Angeles to open a series against the Dodgers Wednesday at 7:10 PM PT.

watchlist: FOMC decision Wednesday, July 29, 2 PM ET — Fed Chair Kevin Warsh expected to hold rates at 3.50%-3.75%, though futures still price roughly a 1-in-3 chance of a hike
Microsoft and Meta report earnings Wednesday, Apple and Amazon Thursday — capex guidance is the key number after Alphabet's spending disclosures helped trigger this week's chip selloff
CPI report (July data) — Wednesday, August 12, 8:30 AM ET
Mariners at Dodgers — Wednesday 7:10 PM PT, Dodger Stadium
Jalen Duren restricted free agency stalemate with the Pistons remains unresolved

deepDive.title: Why 'Correction' and 'Capex Discipline' Are the Two Words Driving Today's Selloff
content: Today's Nasdaq 100 slide into correction - roughly 10% below its recent record - is really a story about one accounting question hanging over the entire AI trade: are hyperscalers' capital expenditures actually generating matching revenue, or is the market simply rewarding the spending itself? Dell falling 8% and Intel falling 6% in a single session looks disconnected from company-specific news, but it reflects a broader repricing of every name whose earnings depend on ever-larger AI infrastructure buildouts. With Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and Amazon all reporting within 48 hours, this week is when that question gets tested against real numbers rather than investor anxiety.

When a company builds a data center full of GPUs, it doesn't expense that cost immediately - it capitalizes the spending as a long-lived asset and depreciates it over several years, typically three to six for compute hardware given rapid obsolescence. That accounting choice matters enormously: it lets a company report strong near-term profits even while spending tens of billions on infrastructure, because the cash outflow hits the balance sheet as capex while the income statement only absorbs a fraction of the cost each year as depreciation. The catch is that depreciation is a bet on useful life and utilization - if GPUs get replaced faster than assumed, or run at lower utilization than modeled, the same spending produces a bigger drag on future earnings than today's numbers suggest.

This is precisely the dynamic that inflated, and then punished, telecom capex in the late 1990s: companies capitalized massive fiber-optic buildouts on assumptions about traffic growth that proved wildly optimistic, and when growth undershot, the same assets that had powered reported earnings turned into write-downs that erased them. Alphabet's capex guidance last week rattled markets not because the dollar figure was shocking on its own, but because it revised the multi-year spending trajectory upward without a matching upward revision to disclosed AI revenue - the exact gap that turned 1990s fiber buildouts from growth story to write-down. Meta routing its new Texas data center through a joint venture with BlackRock, rather than fully owning it, is itself a signal that hyperscalers are structuring spending to keep it from hitting their own free cash flow directly.

For a portfolio watching this week's calendar, the read-through is straightforward: Wednesday's and Thursday's earnings will show whether Microsoft, Meta, Apple, and Amazon can point to AI-driven revenue growing at least as fast as their capex commitments, or whether they're following Alphabet's pattern of spending guidance outrunning monetization proof. That question matters more for the Nasdaq 100's next move than Wednesday's Fed decision, where a hold is already close to fully priced. Watch the language around capex specifically, not the headline revenue or EPS beat, since that's the number that actually moved markets into this correction - and the one that can pull the index back out of it.
